questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Maximum and Minimum Values of a Quadratic Form on the Unit Sphere
questions.problem: Find the maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}=3.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Minimum Value Given a Canonical Form on the Unit Sphere
questions.problem: Find the minimum value of $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${x}_{1}^{2}\ge 0.$ So, we have that

$$
3{x}_{1}^{2}\ge -2{x}_{1}^{2}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & \ge -2{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-2({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $‖x‖=1$ is equivalent to ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=1.$ So,  

$$
\begin{aligned}-2({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2})=-2(1)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

and, in turn, $Q(x)\ge -2.$

So, the value of $Q(x)$ can be no smaller than $-2.$ But before we conclude that $-2$ is the minimum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(x)=-2.$

Notice that when $x={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =3(0)^{2}-2(1)^{2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, given that $‖x‖=1,$ the minimum value of $Q(x)$ is equal to $-2.$

Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that:

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-9) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(\lambda -4)(\lambda +2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-1,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}=-2.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Maximum Value Given a Canonical Form on the Unit Sphere
questions.problem: Find the maximum value of $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+4{x}_{3}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${x}_{1}^{2}\ge 0$ and ${x}_{3}^{2}\ge 0.$ So, we have that

$$
3{x}_{1}^{2}\le 6{x}_{1}^{2},\,4{x}_{3}^{2}\le 6{x}_{3}^{2}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+4{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & \le 6{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+6{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =6({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $‖x‖=1$ is equivalent to ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}=1.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}6({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2})=6(1)=6.\end{aligned}
$$

and, in turn, $Q(x)\le 6.$ 

So, the value of $Q(x)$ can be no greater than $6.$ But before we conclude that $6$ is the maximum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(x)=6.$

Notice that when $x={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+4{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =3(0)^{2}+6(1)^{2}+4(0)^{2} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, given that $‖x‖=1,$ the maximum value of  $Q(x)$ is equal to $6.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Minimum Value Given a Canonical Form on the Unit Sphere
questions.problem: Find the minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${x}_{1}^{2}\ge 0.$ So, we have that

$$
4{x}_{1}^{2}\ge -6{x}_{1}^{2}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =4{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & \ge -6{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-6({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $‖x‖=1$ is equivalent to ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=1.$ So,  

$$
\begin{aligned}-6({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2})=-6(1)=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

and, in turn, $Q(x)\ge -6.$

So, the value of $Q(x)$ can be no smaller than $-6.$ But before we conclude that $-6$ is the minimum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(x)=-6.$

Notice that when $x={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =4{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4(0)^{2}-6(1)^{2} \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, given that $‖x‖=1,$ the minimum value of $Q(x)$ is equal to $-6.$
